# Object-oriented programming {#sec-ch-oop}

> *"I thought of objects being like biological cells and/or individual computers
> on a network, only able to communicate with messages."* — Alan Kay
> [@kay2003].

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- explain the ideas behind object-oriented programming (OOP) — **abstraction,
  encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism** — and where they come from;
- define **classes** with attributes and methods, create **objects**, and
  explain `self`, bound methods and attribute lookup;
- protect an object's **invariants** with encapsulation and **properties**;
- implement **special methods** (`__init__`, `__repr__`, `__str__`, `__eq__`,
  `__hash__`, `__lt__`, `__len__`, …) and state the mathematical laws they must
  obey;
- document classes with **docstrings**;
- use **inheritance**, `super()`, **polymorphism** and abstract base classes;
  apply the **Liskov substitution principle**; compute the **method
  resolution order** with the C3 algorithm;
- choose between inheritance and **composition**, and use `@dataclass`,
  `@classmethod` and `@staticmethod`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Topics covered
Classes and objects; special methods; docstrings; inheritance and polymorphism.
:::

## Intuition: blueprints and houses

A **class** is a blueprint; an **object** (or *instance*) is a house built
from it. From one blueprint you can build many houses; each house has its own
state (the colour of its walls, who lives there), but all share the same
structure and the same "things you can do" (open the door, turn on the lights).

- The **state** of an object is stored in its **attributes** (data).
- Its **behaviour** is given by its **methods** (functions attached to the
  class).

Procedural programming (@sec-ch-functions) organises a program around
*actions* operating on data passed around. OOP bundles each kind of data with
the operations allowed on it, so that the rest of the program interacts with
the data **only through those operations**. That bundle is the unit of
design.

## A short history of the ideas {#sec-oop-history .deep}

- **Simula 67** (Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard, Norwegian Computing
  Center) introduced classes, objects, inheritance and virtual methods, to
  write *simulations* of systems made of interacting entities
  [@dahl1966; @dahl1968].
- **Abstract data types** (Barbara Liskov and Stephen Zilles, 1974): a type is
  defined by the operations on it, not by its representation [@liskov1974].
- **Information hiding** (David Parnas, 1972): hide each design decision likely
  to change behind an interface (@sec-ch-modules) [@parnas1972].
- **Smalltalk** (Alan Kay and colleagues at Xerox PARC, 1970s) coined the term
  *object-oriented* and pushed the model of objects communicating through
  **messages** [@kay1993].
- **C++** (1985), **Java** (1995) and **Python** (1991) brought OOP to the
  mainstream; the *Design Patterns* book (the "Gang of Four", 1994) catalogued
  recurring object designs [@gamma1994].

## Classes and objects {#sec-classes}

### A first class

::: {#62dba521 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
class Contact:
    """A person in a phone book."""

    country_code_default = 39            # CLASS attribute: shared by all instances

    def __init__(self, name, surname, phone):
        # INSTANCE attributes: each object has its own
        self.name = name
        self.surname = surname
        self.phone = phone

    def full_name(self):                 # a METHOD
        return f"{self.name} {self.surname}"

ada = Contact("Ada", "Lovelace", "+44 20 0000")    # creating an instance calls __init__
alan = Contact("Alan", "Turing", "+44 161 0000")
print(ada.full_name(), "|", alan.full_name())
print(type(ada), isinstance(ada, Contact), ada.country_code_default)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
Ada Lovelace | Alan Turing
<class '__main__.Contact'> True 39
```
:::
:::


What happens in `Contact("Ada", "Lovelace", …)`:

1. Python creates a new, empty object of type `Contact` (method `__new__`);
2. it calls `__init__` with the new object as first argument, followed by your
   arguments; `__init__` **initialises** the attributes;
3. the expression evaluates to the new object.

### `self` and bound methods

Methods are ordinary functions defined in the class body. Their first
parameter, by convention named `self`, receives the instance. When you write
`ada.full_name()`, Python looks up `full_name` on the class and creates a
**bound method** that remembers `ada`; calling it passes `ada` as `self`. The
two calls below are therefore identical:

::: {#8b035494 .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
print(ada.full_name())
print(Contact.full_name(ada))      # what Python actually does
print(ada.full_name)               # a bound method object
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
Ada Lovelace
Ada Lovelace
<bound method Contact.full_name of <__main__.Contact object at 0x7f21b557d2b0>>
```
:::
:::


### Attribute lookup

Each instance stores its attributes in a dictionary, `obj.__dict__`
(@sec-dicts). Reading `obj.attr` looks first in the **instance** dictionary,
then in the **class**, then in its **base classes** in method-resolution order
(@sec-mro). Assignment `obj.attr = value` always writes into the instance.

::: {#189b2326 .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
print(ada.__dict__)
ada.country_code_default = 44                  # creates an INSTANCE attribute that shadows the class one
print(ada.country_code_default, alan.country_code_default, Contact.country_code_default)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
{'name': 'Ada', 'surname': 'Lovelace', 'phone': '+44 20 0000'}
44 39 39
```
:::
:::


::: {.callout-warning}
## Class attributes that are mutable
A class attribute such as `contacts = []` is **shared by all instances**: one
`append` through any instance changes it for all — the class-level twin of the
mutable-default trap (@sec-mutable-default). Initialise per-instance state in
`__init__`.
:::

## Encapsulation and invariants {#sec-encapsulation}

An object usually has **invariants**: conditions on its state that must always
hold — a bank balance is never negative, a contact always has a non-empty
name. Bertrand Meyer called these **class invariants** and made them part of
*Design by Contract* [@meyer1997]: every public method may assume the invariant
on entry and must restore it on exit. Encapsulation is what makes this
possible: if outside code can modify the attributes directly, nobody can
guarantee anything.

Python does not enforce privacy; it relies on conventions [@pep8]:

- `name` — public;
- `_name` — internal: "please don't touch from outside";
- `__name` — *name mangling*: inside class `C` it becomes `_C__name`, to avoid
  accidental clashes in subclasses (not a security mechanism).

The Pythonic tool for controlled access is the **property**: an attribute
whose reads and writes go through methods.

::: {#9425037f .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
class BankAccount:
    """A bank account whose balance can never become negative (class invariant)."""

    def __init__(self, owner: str, balance: float = 0.0):
        if balance < 0:
            raise ValueError("initial balance must be >= 0")
        self.owner = owner
        self._balance = balance              # internal: modified only by methods

    @property
    def balance(self) -> float:              # read-only from outside
        return self._balance

    def deposit(self, amount: float) -> None:
        if amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("deposit must be positive")
        self._balance += amount              # preserves balance >= 0

    def withdraw(self, amount: float) -> None:
        if not 0 < amount <= self._balance:
            raise ValueError("invalid amount or insufficient funds")
        self._balance -= amount              # preserves balance >= 0

acct = BankAccount("Ada", 100)
acct.deposit(50); acct.withdraw(30)
print(acct.balance)
try:
    acct.balance = 1_000_000                 # no setter: the property is read-only
except AttributeError as err:
    print("AttributeError:", err)
try:
    acct.withdraw(500)
except ValueError as err:
    print("ValueError:", err)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
120
AttributeError: property 'balance' of 'BankAccount' object has no setter
ValueError: invalid amount or insufficient funds
```
:::
:::


::: {#prp-invariant-preserved}
## The invariant always holds
For any sequence of calls to `__init__`, `deposit` and `withdraw` that do not
raise, `acct.balance >= 0` after each call (assuming no code touches
`_balance` directly).
:::

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-invariant-preserved
Induction on the number of calls. After `__init__`, $b = \text{balance} \ge 0$
because negative values raise. If $b \ge 0$ before `deposit(a)`, the method
either raises (state unchanged) or $a > 0$ and the new balance is $b + a > 0$.
Before `withdraw(a)`, either it raises (unchanged) or $0 < a \le b$, and the
new balance is $b - a \ge 0$. Since `_balance` is modified only in these three
places, the invariant holds after every call. $\blacksquare$

This is the loop-invariant technique of @sec-loop-invariants applied to the
*life* of an object: every method is one "iteration".
:::

## Special methods: the Python data model {#sec-special-methods}

Python's syntax is implemented by **special methods** ("dunder" methods, from
*double underscore*). `len(x)` calls `x.__len__()`, `a + b` calls
`a.__add__(b)`, `a == b` calls `a.__eq__(b)`, `print(x)` calls
`x.__str__()`, and so on. By defining them, your classes behave like
built-in types. The full list is in the Language Reference, §3.3 *Special
method names* [@pythonreference].

| You write | Python calls | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `C(args)` | `__init__(self, args)` | initialise |
| `repr(x)` | `__repr__(self)` | unambiguous text for developers |
| `str(x)`, `print(x)` | `__str__(self)` | readable text for users |
| `x == y` | `__eq__(self, y)` | equality |
| `hash(x)` | `__hash__(self)` | for sets and dict keys (@sec-hash-contract) |
| `x < y` | `__lt__(self, y)` | ordering (used by `sorted`) |
| `len(x)` | `__len__(self)` | size |
| `bool(x)`, `if x:` | `__bool__(self)` (else `__len__`) | truthiness |
| `item in x` | `__contains__(self, item)` | membership |
| `for i in x` | `__iter__(self)` | iteration (@sec-iteration-protocol) |
| `x[k]` | `__getitem__(self, k)` | indexing |
| `x + y` | `__add__(self, y)` | arithmetic |

: Some special methods {#tbl-dunder}

::: {#6eef120a .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from functools import total_ordering

@total_ordering                    # derives <=, >, >= from __eq__ and __lt__
class Contact:
    def __init__(self, name, surname, phone):
        self.name, self.surname, self.phone = name, surname, phone

    def __repr__(self):            # for developers: looks like code that rebuilds the object
        return f"Contact({self.name!r}, {self.surname!r}, {self.phone!r})"

    def __str__(self):             # for users
        return f"{self.surname}, {self.name}: {self.phone}"

    def _key(self):
        return (self.surname.lower(), self.name.lower(), self.phone)

    def __eq__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Contact):
            return NotImplemented  # let Python try other.__eq__ or fall back to identity
        return self._key() == other._key()

    def __hash__(self):            # consistent with __eq__: equal keys -> equal hashes
        return hash(self._key())

    def __lt__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Contact):
            return NotImplemented
        return self._key() < other._key()   # lexicographic: surname, then name, then phone

people = [Contact("Mario", "Rossi", "333"), Contact("anna", "Bianchi", "320"),
          Contact("Anna", "Rossi", "347")]
print(sorted(people))
print(people[0])
print(Contact("Ada", "L", "1") == Contact("ada", "l", "1"),
      len({Contact("Ada", "L", "1"), Contact("ADA", "L", "1")}))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
[Contact('anna', 'Bianchi', '320'), Contact('Anna', 'Rossi', '347'), Contact('Mario', 'Rossi', '333')]
Rossi, Mario: 333
True 1
```
:::
:::


**`NotImplemented`** (a special singleton, not the exception
`NotImplementedError`) tells Python "I don't know how to compare with this
type"; Python then tries the reflected operation on the other operand and, for
`==`, falls back to identity.

Built-in tools **assume** that `__eq__` behaves like a true equality and
`__lt__` like a true order. If they do not, sets, dicts and `sorted`
misbehave silently, without any error. Comparing **key tuples**, as above, is
the safe recipe; the deep dive below states the exact laws and proves why the
recipe works.

### The laws behind `__eq__` and `__lt__` {.deep}

Built-in algorithms *assume* that your methods behave like mathematical
relations. If they do not, sets, dicts and `sorted` silently misbehave.

::: {#def-equivalence}
## Equivalence relation
A relation $\sim$ on a set is an **equivalence** if it is reflexive
($a\sim a$), symmetric ($a\sim b \Rightarrow b\sim a$) and transitive
($a\sim b \wedge b\sim c \Rightarrow a\sim c$).
:::

::: {#def-strict-weak-order}
## Strict order
A relation $<$ is a **strict partial order** if it is irreflexive (never
$a<a$) and transitive. It is a **strict total order** if moreover for all
$a \ne b$ either $a<b$ or $b<a$ (*trichotomy*).
:::

`__eq__` must be an equivalence (and consistent with `__hash__`,
@prp-hash-contract); `__lt__` must be a strict order for `sorted` to return a
meaningful result. Comparing **keys** that are tuples of strings, as above, is
safe because:

::: {#thm-lex-order}
## Lexicographic order is a strict total order
If $<_1$ and $<_2$ are strict total orders on sets $A$ and $B$, then the
lexicographic order on $A\times B$,
$(a,b) < (a',b') \iff a <_1 a' \ \vee\ (a = a' \wedge b <_2 b')$,
is a strict total order. By induction the same holds for tuples of any length.
:::

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-lex-order
*Irreflexive*: $(a,b)<(a,b)$ would need $a<_1 a$ or $b <_2 b$, both false.

*Transitive*: let $(a,b) < (a',b')$ and $(a',b') < (a'',b'')$. If $a <_1 a'$
and $a' <_1 a''$, then $a <_1 a''$. If $a<_1 a'$ and $a' = a''$, then
$a <_1 a''$. If $a = a'$ and $a' <_1 a''$, then $a <_1 a''$. If $a = a' = a''$,
then $b <_2 b'$ and $b' <_2 b''$, so $b <_2 b''$. In all cases
$(a,b) < (a'',b'')$.

*Trichotomy*: let $(a,b)\neq(a',b')$. If $a\ne a'$, trichotomy of $<_1$ gives
$a <_1 a'$ or $a' <_1 a$. If $a = a'$, then $b \ne b'$ and trichotomy of $<_2$
decides. $\blacksquare$
:::

Note what happens if the key is only `(surname, name)`: two different contacts
"Mario Rossi, 333" and "Mario Rossi, 347" are then neither `<` nor `>` each
other. The relation is no longer total — it is a **strict weak order**
(incomparability is an equivalence), which is still fine for sorting: Python's
sort is stable (@def-stable), so such ties keep their insertion order.

## Docstrings {#sec-class-docstrings}

Classes and methods are documented like functions (@sec-docstrings-functions):
the first string in the class body is the class docstring. PEP 257 [@pep257]
suggests summarising the class's behaviour and listing its public methods and
attributes; `help(Class)` renders everything.

::: {#976192af .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
class Rectangle:
    """An axis-aligned rectangle.

    Attributes:
        width: horizontal side length (> 0).
        height: vertical side length (> 0).
    """

    def __init__(self, width: float, height: float):
        """Create a rectangle; raise ValueError if a side is not positive."""
        if width <= 0 or height <= 0:
            raise ValueError("sides must be positive")
        self.width, self.height = width, height

    def area(self) -> float:
        """Return width * height."""
        return self.width * self.height

print(Rectangle.__doc__.splitlines()[0])
print(Rectangle.area.__doc__)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
An axis-aligned rectangle.
Return width * height.
```
:::
:::


## Inheritance and polymorphism {#sec-inheritance}

### Inheritance

A class can **inherit** from another: the **subclass** (child) gets all the
attributes and methods of the **base class** (parent), can **add** new ones and
can **override** existing ones. Inheritance models an **"is-a"** relation: a
`Square` *is a* `Shape`.

::: {#ac23ceec .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import math

class Shape:
    """Base class: every shape has a name and an area."""
    def __init__(self, name: str):
        self.name = name
    def area(self) -> float:
        raise NotImplementedError("subclasses must implement area()")
    def describe(self) -> str:                  # uses area(), whatever the subclass
        return f"{self.name} with area {self.area():.2f}"

class Circle(Shape):
    def __init__(self, r: float):
        super().__init__("circle")              # run the parent's __init__
        self.r = r
    def area(self) -> float:                    # override
        return math.pi * self.r ** 2

class Rect(Shape):
    def __init__(self, w: float, h: float):
        super().__init__("rectangle")
        self.w, self.h = w, h
    def area(self) -> float:
        return self.w * self.h

class Square(Rect):
    def __init__(self, side: float):
        super().__init__(side, side)
        self.name = "square"

shapes = [Circle(1), Rect(2, 3), Square(2)]
for s in shapes:
    print(s.describe())                         # the right area() is chosen at run time
print(isinstance(shapes[2], Rect), issubclass(Square, Shape), Square.__mro__)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
circle with area 3.14
rectangle with area 6.00
square with area 4.00
True True (<class '__main__.Square'>, <class '__main__.Rect'>, <class '__main__.Shape'>, <class 'object'>)
```
:::
:::


`super()` returns a proxy that delegates to the **next class in the method
resolution order** (@sec-mro) — usually the parent.

### Polymorphism

`describe` calls `self.area()` without knowing which subclass `self` belongs
to; the method actually executed is chosen **at run time** from the object's
class (*dynamic dispatch*). This is **subtype polymorphism** (*poly-morph*:
"many forms"): one interface, many implementations. Code written against the
`Shape` interface works for shapes that did not exist when it was written —
this is the *open–closed principle* ("open for extension, closed for
modification") of Bertrand Meyer [@meyer1997].

Python also has **duck typing** — *"if it walks like a duck and quacks like a
duck, it is a duck"*: any object with an `area()` method works with a function
that calls `.area()`, inheritance or not. The `for` loop's iteration protocol
and `len()` are duck-typed.

### The Liskov substitution principle {#sec-lsp}

When is inheritance *correct*? Barbara Liskov gave the answer in her 1987
keynote, formalised with Jeannette Wing [@liskov1994]:

::: {#def-lsp}
## Liskov substitution principle (LSP)
Let $\phi(x)$ be a property provable about objects $x$ of type $T$. Then
$\phi(y)$ should be true for objects $y$ of type $S$, where $S$ is a subtype
of $T$.
:::

In practice: a subclass must **honour the contract** of its parent — accept at
least the same inputs (preconditions may only be weakened), guarantee at least
the same results (postconditions may only be strengthened), and preserve the
parent's invariants.

::: {#exm-square-rectangle}
## The square–rectangle problem
Suppose `Rect` had a method `set_width(w)` with the postcondition "width
becomes `w`, height is unchanged". A `Square` must keep `width == height`, so
its `set_width` must also change the height — **violating** the parent's
postcondition. Code like
```python
def stretch(r: Rect):
    r.set_width(2 * r.w)
    assert r.area() == 2 * old_area   # true for every Rect, false for a Square
```
breaks when given a `Square`. Geometrically a square *is* a rectangle; but a
*mutable* `Square` object is not a substitutable *mutable* `Rect` object.
Remedies: make the shapes immutable (our version above has no setters), or do
not derive `Square` from `Rect`.
:::

### Abstract base classes

`Shape.area` above raises `NotImplementedError` at *call* time. The `abc`
module (PEP 3119 [@pep3119]) lets you declare **abstract methods**, so that
instantiating an incomplete class fails immediately:

::: {#0ac6ee81 .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Storage(ABC):
    """Interface: where a phone book can be saved."""
    @abstractmethod
    def save(self, records: list[dict]) -> None: ...
    @abstractmethod
    def load(self) -> list[dict]: ...

class MemoryStorage(Storage):
    def __init__(self):
        self._data = []
    def save(self, records):
        self._data = [dict(r) for r in records]
    def load(self):
        return [dict(r) for r in self._data]

try:
    Storage()
except TypeError as err:
    print("TypeError:", err)
m = MemoryStorage(); m.save([{"name": "Ada"}]); print(m.load())
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class Storage without an implementation for abstract methods 'load', 'save'
[{'name': 'Ada'}]
```
:::
:::


A class may also have **several** base classes. Python then looks for methods
in a fixed order, the **method resolution order** (MRO), visible as
`Class.__mro__`, and `super()` follows that order. The deep dive below explains
how the order is computed.

### Multiple inheritance and the method resolution order {#sec-mro .deep}

Python allows a class to inherit from several bases. Then a question arises:
when a method is defined in more than one ancestor, **which one is used?** The
answer is the **method resolution order** (MRO), a linear ordering of the
class and its ancestors, available as `Class.__mro__`. Since Python 2.3 the MRO
is computed with the **C3 linearisation**, proposed for the Dylan language by
Barrett et al. [@barrett1996] and adopted for Python by Samuele Pedroni and
documented by Michele Simionato [@simionato2003].

::: {#def-c3}
## C3 linearisation
For a class $C$ with bases $B_1, \dots, B_k$ (in the order written in the
class statement), its linearisation $L[C]$ is
$$
L[C] = C + \operatorname{merge}\big(L[B_1], \dots, L[B_k],\ [B_1,\dots,B_k]\big),\qquad L[\texttt{object}] = [\texttt{object}],
$$
where **merge** repeatedly takes the first **head** (first element) of the
lists that does **not** appear in the **tail** (any position but the first) of
any list, appends it to the result and removes it from all lists. If no such
head exists, the hierarchy is rejected.
:::

::: {#exm-c3-diamond}
## The diamond
`class A`, `class B(A)`, `class C(A)`, `class D(B, C)`. Write $O$ for
`object`. $L[A] = [A, O]$, $L[B] = [B, A, O]$, $L[C] = [C, A, O]$.
$$
\begin{aligned}
L[D] &= D + \operatorname{merge}([B,A,O],\,[C,A,O],\,[B,C])\\
&= D, B + \operatorname{merge}([A,O],\,[C,A,O],\,[C]) && B \text{ is in no tail}\\
&= D, B, C + \operatorname{merge}([A,O],\,[A,O]) && A \text{ is in the tail of } [C,A,O]\text{: skip; take } C\\
&= D, B, C, A, O .
\end{aligned}
$$
`A` comes after **both** `B` and `C`: a method of `A` is used only if neither
`B` nor `C` overrides it.
:::

::: {#aba81fd3 .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
class A:
    def hello(self): return "A"
class B(A):
    def hello(self): return "B -> " + super().hello()
class C(A):
    def hello(self): return "C -> " + super().hello()
class D(B, C):
    def hello(self): return "D -> " + super().hello()

print([k.__name__ for k in D.__mro__])
print(D().hello())               # super() follows the MRO, not just "the parent"

try:
    class X(A, B):               # A before B, but B is a subclass of A: inconsistent
        pass
except TypeError as err:
    print("TypeError:", err)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
['D', 'B', 'C', 'A', 'object']
D -> B -> C -> A
TypeError: Cannot create a consistent method resolution order (MRO) for bases A, B
```
:::
:::


Note how `super()` in `B` called `C`, not `A`: it delegates to the *next class
in the MRO of the object's class*. This is what makes **cooperative multiple
inheritance** work: each class calls `super()` once and every class in the
diamond runs exactly once.

::: {#prp-c3-properties}
## Guarantees of C3
If $L[C]$ exists, then (a) every class appears before all of its bases
(**local precedence**: bases also appear in the order listed); and (b)
$L[C]$ extends the linearisation of each base, i.e. the relative order of the
classes in $L[B_i]$ is preserved in $L[C]$ (**monotonicity**).
:::

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-c3-properties
Both properties follow from one invariant of **merge**: *an element is output
only when it is the head of every list that contains it.* Indeed, it is chosen
only if it appears in no tail; so in every list where it appears, it is at the
head. Consequently, if $x$ precedes $y$ in some input list, $y$ cannot be
output before $x$: while $x$ is still present, $y$ is in the tail of that list.
Hence merge preserves the order of every input list.
(a) The last input list is $[B_1,\dots,B_k]$, so the bases appear in the listed
order; and $C$ itself is placed first. Applying the same argument recursively
to each $L[B_i]$ shows that every class precedes its own bases.
(b) Each $L[B_i]$ is an input list of the merge, so its order is preserved.
$\blacksquare$

If the constraints are contradictory (as in `class X(A, B)` with `B` a
subclass of `A`: the list $[A, B]$ demands $A$ before $B$, while $L[B]$
demands $B$ before $A$), merge gets stuck and Python raises `TypeError`, as the
code shows.
:::

## Composition over inheritance {#sec-composition}

Inheritance couples the subclass tightly to the parent's implementation. The
*Design Patterns* authors summarised decades of experience in one principle:
**"Favor object composition over class inheritance"** [@gamma1994]. In
composition, an object **has** other objects (a **"has-a"** relation) and
delegates work to them.

A phone book *is not* a list (it should not expose `pop`, `sort`, `insert` to
arbitrary callers), but it *has* a collection of contacts:

::: {#fbe6c9cc .cell execution_count=10}
``` {.python .cell-code}
class PhoneBook:
    """A collection of unique contacts (composition: it HAS a dict)."""
    def __init__(self):
        self._by_key = {}                       # key -> Contact; O(1) duplicate check
    def add(self, contact: Contact) -> bool:
        key = contact._key()
        if key in self._by_key:
            return False                        # invariant: no duplicates
        self._by_key[key] = contact
        return True
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self._by_key)
    def __iter__(self):                         # iterate in sorted order
        return iter(sorted(self._by_key.values()))
    def search(self, text: str):
        t = text.lower()
        return [c for c in self if t in c.name.lower() or t in c.surname.lower()]

book = PhoneBook()
for c in people + [Contact("Mario", "Rossi", "333")]:   # the last one is a duplicate
    book.add(c)
print(len(book), [str(c) for c in book])
print(book.search("ross"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
3 ['Bianchi, anna: 320', 'Rossi, Anna: 347', 'Rossi, Mario: 333']
[Contact('Anna', 'Rossi', '347'), Contact('Mario', 'Rossi', '333')]
```
:::

## Dataclasses, class methods and static methods {#sec-dataclasses}

Writing `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` by hand is repetitive. The
`dataclasses` module (PEP 557 [@pep557]) generates them from **annotated class
attributes**:

::: {#3fb6de12 .cell execution_count=11}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from dataclasses import dataclass, field, asdict

@dataclass(order=True, frozen=True)      # order: generates __lt__ etc.; frozen: immutable & hashable
class Person:
    surname: str
    name: str
    phone: str = field(compare=False)     # excluded from ==, <, hash

    @classmethod
    def from_dict(cls, d: dict) -> "Person":     # alternative constructor
        return cls(d["surname"], d["name"], d["phone"])

    @staticmethod
    def is_valid_phone(text: str) -> bool:       # utility: needs neither self nor cls
        digits = text.replace(" ", "").lstrip("+")
        return digits.isdigit() and 6 <= len(digits) <= 15

p = Person.from_dict({"surname": "Hopper", "name": "Grace", "phone": "+1 202 555 0100"})
print(p, asdict(p), Person.is_valid_phone(p.phone))
print(sorted([Person("Rossi", "Mario", "1"), Person("Bianchi", "Anna", "2")]))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
Person(surname='Hopper', name='Grace', phone='+1 202 555 0100') {'surname': 'Hopper', 'name': 'Grace', 'phone': '+1 202 555 0100'} True
[Person(surname='Bianchi', name='Anna', phone='2'), Person(surname='Rossi', name='Mario', phone='1')]
```
:::
:::


- A **class method** (`@classmethod`) receives the class as `cls`: ideal for
  alternative constructors (`from_dict`, `from_json`), and it works correctly
  for subclasses.
- A **static method** (`@staticmethod`) receives neither the instance nor the
  class: a plain function placed in the class namespace for organisation.

The limit of 15 digits in `is_valid_phone` comes from the ITU-T E.164
numbering plan, which caps international numbers at 15 digits [@itue164].

## Design principles in one table {#sec-solid}

| Principle | Meaning | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Single responsibility | a class should have one reason to change | @martin2003 |
| Open–closed | extend behaviour by adding code, not changing it | @meyer1997 |
| Liskov substitution | subclasses must honour the parent's contract | @liskov1994 |
| Interface segregation | many small interfaces beat one large one | @martin2003 |
| Dependency inversion | depend on abstractions (e.g. `Storage`), not concretions | @martin2003 |
| Composition over inheritance | prefer *has-a* to *is-a* when in doubt | @gamma1994 |
| Information hiding | hide decisions likely to change | @parnas1972 |

The first five are known by the acronym **SOLID**.

::: {.project-link}
**In the project.** Requirements R2 and R3 (@sec-project-brief) ask for one
class for a single contact, one for the collection, and the user interaction
kept outside both — i.e. the **single-responsibility** principle. The implementation in `ai-projects`
defines `Contatto` (with `__init__`, `__eq__` comparing all four fields, and
`__lt__` comparing `(surname, name)` tuples — a strict weak order,
@thm-lex-order) and `Rubrica`, which *has* a list of contacts (composition).
Reading it with this chapter in mind suggests concrete improvements, discussed
in @sec-ch-project-phonebook: (1) `__eq__` without `__hash__` makes contacts
**unhashable**, so they cannot be put in a set or used as dict keys
(@prp-hash-contract); (2) `Rubrica` reads `contatto._nome` directly, bypassing
encapsulation — properties or public read-only attributes would be cleaner;
(3) `input_valid_contact` is defined without `self` and called on the class:
it should be a `@staticmethod` (or, better, live outside the domain class,
since it does I/O); (4) a `@classmethod from_dict` would make JSON loading
symmetric with saving.
:::

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out
- **Forgetting `self`** in a method definition (`def area():`) →
  `TypeError: … takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given`.
- **Mutable class attributes** shared by all instances.
- **Defining `__eq__` without `__hash__`** → instances become unhashable; or
  defining `__hash__` inconsistently with `__eq__` → sets and dicts break.
- **Comparisons that are not orders** (e.g. `__lt__` based on `<=`) → `sorted`
  produces garbage without any error.
- **Deep inheritance hierarchies** for code reuse: prefer composition.
- **Subclasses that break the parent's contract** (LSP violations).
- **Calling the parent's `__init__` by name** (`Parent.__init__(self)`) in
  multiple inheritance: use `super()` consistently.
:::

## Summary

- A class bundles data (attributes) and behaviour (methods); `self` is the
  instance, passed automatically through bound methods.
- Encapsulation (conventions, properties) lets a class guarantee its
  **invariants**, proved like loop invariants.
- Special methods integrate classes with Python syntax; `__eq__` must be an
  equivalence consistent with `__hash__`, `__lt__` a strict (weak) order.
- Inheritance models *is-a*; polymorphism picks the method at run time;
  correct subclasses obey the **Liskov substitution principle**.
- The MRO is computed by **C3**, which preserves local precedence and
  monotonicity; `super()` follows the MRO.
- Prefer composition; use `@dataclass`, `@classmethod`, `@staticmethod` to
  remove boilerplate.

## Exercises

::: {#exr-ch7-fraction}
Implement a class `Fraction(num, den)` that always stores the fraction in
lowest terms with a positive denominator (use `math.gcd`), with `__repr__`,
`__eq__`, `__hash__`, `__lt__`, `__add__`, `__mul__`. State the class
invariant and argue that each method preserves it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Invariant: `den > 0` and `gcd(|num|, den) == 1`. Normalise in `__init__`
(divide by the gcd, move the sign to the numerator; reject `den == 0`); every
arithmetic method builds its result through `__init__`, so the invariant holds
by construction. Then equality of values is equality of `(num, den)`, so
`__hash__ = hash((num, den))` respects the contract;
`a/b < c/d \iff ad < cb` since $b,d>0$. (The standard library has
`fractions.Fraction`.)
:::

::: {#exr-ch7-mro}
Compute by hand, with C3, the MRO of `class Z(K1, K2, K3)` where
`class K1(A, B, C)`, `class K2(D, B, E)`, `class K3(D, A)`, and `A`…`E` derive
from `object`. Check with Python.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
$L[K1] = K1,A,B,C,O$; $L[K2] = K2,D,B,E,O$; $L[K3] = K3,D,A,O$. Merging with
$[K1,K2,K3]$: $Z, K1, K2, K3, D, A, B, C, E, O$ (this is the example worked out in @simionato2003).
:::

::: {#exr-ch7-lsp}
Give an example of a subclass that violates LSP by **strengthening a
precondition**, and explain which client code breaks.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
`class Account: def withdraw(self, amount)` accepts any `0 < amount <= balance`.
`class LimitedAccount(Account)` raises if `amount > 100`. A client that, given
any `Account` with enough balance, withdraws 150 works for `Account` and fails
for `LimitedAccount`: the subclass demands more from its callers.
:::

::: {#exr-ch7-iter}
Make `PhoneBook` support `"Ada" in book` (search by name) and `book["Rossi"]`
(list of contacts with that surname) by implementing `__contains__` and
`__getitem__`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```python
def __contains__(self, name):
    return any(c.name == name for c in self._by_key.values())
def __getitem__(self, surname):
    return [c for c in self if c.surname == surname]
```
:::
